column1: Enable memory-optimized storage with {{c1::MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON}} in the CREATE TABLE options.
column2:
The option chooses the memory-optimized table structure. On SQL Server, prepare the required memory-optimized filegroup before creating the table.
Review source

column1: For durable memory-optimized storage, use WITH (MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON, DURABILITY = {{c1::SCHEMA_AND_DATA}}).
column2:
SCHEMA_AND_DATA preserves both the definition and committed rows through normal recovery. Active data still resides in memory while the database runs.
Review source

column1: The memory-optimized durability option that persists only the table definition is DURABILITY = {{c1::SCHEMA_ONLY}}.
column2:
SCHEMA_ONLY recreates the table definition after restart but does not restore its former rows. Use it only when the data can be lost or rebuilt.
Review source

column1: A system-versioned temporal table requires two period columns of type {{c1::DATETIME2}}.
column2:
Both DATETIME2 columns describe the interval when a version is current. They are system timestamps rather than separate business dates.
Review source

column1: Define a temporal period's start column with ValidFrom DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS {{c1::ROW START}}.
column2:
The ROW START declaration tells SQL Server which column records when the version becomes valid. The engine maintains that value.
Review source

column1: Define a temporal period's end column with ValidTo DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS {{c1::ROW END}}.
column2:
ROW END records when the version stops being valid. A closed history version has a finite end time, while a current version uses the open-ended maximum.
Review source

column1: Associate temporal period columns with {{c1::PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME}} (ValidFrom, ValidTo).
column2:
The clause pairs the two generated columns. Declaring the columns alone does not tell SQL Server that they form the system-time period.
Review source

column1: Enable automatic temporal row versioning with WITH ({{c1::SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON}}).
column2:
SYSTEM_VERSIONING turns on history management. The current table and any named history table must already satisfy the applicable temporal rules.
Review source

column1: To retrieve employee versions that were valid at one UTC instant, use FOR SYSTEM_TIME {{c1::AS OF}} '2026-01-01T00:00:00'.
column2:
AS OF returns the version valid at one UTC instant. It can read a historical version even when the current employee row now contains different data.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2017 and later, omitting a temporal table's HISTORY_RETENTION_PERIOD defaults retention to {{c1::INFINITE}}.
column2:
INFINITE does not remove history based on its age. Set a finite policy and enable cleanup if the database must age out old versions.
Review source

column1: Define a SQL table over external data with the {{c1::CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE}} statement.
column2:
The statement creates a definition in the database, not a durable copy of the external rows. Queries use that definition to access the source.
Review source

column1: In a SQL Server file-based external table, {{c1::LOCATION}} specifies the file or folder path within the source.
column2:
LOCATION selects a path under the external data source. Change the data source when the root or connection must change.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::DATA_SOURCE}} option names the external data source used by a SQL Server external table.
column2:
DATA_SOURCE points to a named object that describes the external location. LOCATION can then identify the relevant path within it.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::FILE_FORMAT}} option names the external file format object used by a file-based external table.
column2:
FILE_FORMAT refers to an external file format object. The object tells the engine how to interpret files, for example which format or text delimiters they use.
Review source

column1: SQL Server ledger tables are available starting with {{c1::SQL Server 2022}}.
column2:
SQL Server 2022 introduced ledger on the boxed product. Do not assume a SQL Server 2019 instance can create a ledger table.
Review source

column1: Enable an updatable ledger table with CREATE TABLE options WITH ({{c1::LEDGER = ON}}).
column2:
LEDGER = ON creates an updatable ledger table unless you request append-only behavior. Such a table allows ordinary DML and preserves old versions.
Review source

column1: Create append-only ledger storage with WITH (LEDGER = ON ({{c1::APPEND_ONLY = ON}})).
column2:
APPEND_ONLY changes which operations the ledger table accepts. New records can be inserted, but existing records cannot be updated or deleted through ordinary DML.
Review source

column1: SQL Server calls the trusted reference based on the latest ledger block hash a {{c1::database digest}}.
column2:
The digest acts as a trusted reference for a later verification. Store it separately so it is not replaced along with altered data.
Review source

column1: Create a graph node table with CREATE TABLE dbo.Person (PersonID INT, Name NVARCHAR(100)) {{c1::AS NODE}};
column2:
AS NODE gives each entity row a generated graph identifier. PersonID can remain a separate identifier for the application.
Review source

column1: Create a graph edge table with CREATE TABLE dbo.Knows {{c1::AS EDGE}};
column2:
AS EDGE gives the table the graph columns that connect two node rows. Add user-defined columns only if the relationship needs its own attributes.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph pseudo-column {{c1::$node_id}} uniquely identifies a node in the database.
column2:
Use $node_id to identify a node in graph operations. The underlying generated internal column name is not the public interface.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph pseudo-column {{c1::$edge_id}} uniquely identifies an edge in the database.
column2:
The edge ID identifies the relationship itself. Its source and target nodes are identified separately by $from_id and $to_id.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph edge pseudo-column {{c1::$from_id}} identifies the node where the edge originates.
column2:
$from_id points to the source node. For Alice knows Bob, it contains Alice's graph identifier.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph edge pseudo-column {{c1::$to_id}} identifies the node where the edge terminates.
column2:
$to_id points to the destination node. For Alice knows Bob, it contains Bob's graph identifier.
Review source

column1: SQL Graph edges are {{c1::directed}} relationships between two nodes.
column2:
An edge from Alice to Bob does not automatically add an edge from Bob to Alice. The endpoint columns preserve the two roles.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::MATCH}} predicate expresses SQL Graph traversal patterns in a WHERE clause.
column2:
MATCH connects aliases in a path pattern. It can express traversal such as one Person connected to another through a Knows edge.
Review source
